title: Polish Locative Case: Endings, Rules and Examples
excerpt: The Polish locative case (miejscownik) always follows w, na, o, przy or po. Learn the endings, consonant changes, pronouns and city names.
metaDescription: The Polish locative case (miejscownik) always follows w, na, o, przy or po. Learn the endings, consonant changes, pronouns and city names, with practice.
summary: The Polish locative case (miejscownik) only ever appears after a preposition: w, na, o, przy or po.
In the singular, hard stems take -e with a consonant change (stół → stole, miasto → mieście), while k/g/ch and soft stems take -u (park → parku, hotel → hotelu).
Feminine nouns take -e, -i or -y, with k → c and g → dz before -e (Polska → w Polsce, noga → na nodze), and the plural is -ach for every gender.
Adjectives end in -ym/-im, -ej or -ych/-ich, and pronouns become o mnie, o tobie, o nim, o niej, o nas, o was, o nich.

factNotes: Not checked individually on Wiktionary but standard, so left in: Lublin and Szczecin locatives (taken from the site's own polish-cities page), historia → o historii, film → o filmie, Marek → o Marku, wakacje → o wakacjach, kanapa → na kanapie, centrum → w centrum, the dative 'kotu', and 'w Chicago / w Toronto' (indeclinable, hedged with 'usually'). Wiktionary also lists archaic or regional 'domie' and 'synie', so the article says only that the standard forms are w domu and o synu.
